answer.answer:
**Summary**

The one causal path to site safety that the evidence actually asserts is moving work off the site: prefabrication and off-site production improves site safety, and it is the only inbound path to that value in the record. Where the robot stays on site and works beside people, safety is handled not as an outcome but as a set of preconditions on human-robot interaction: compliance with robot safety standards, a trained workforce, and power-and-force-limiting operation kept within biomechanical limits to reduce contact injury. Prefabrication is not free either: it requires precise up-front planning and logistics, and third-party certification and traceability for off-site compliance. Watch that the deployed drilling and earthmoving processes in the record were adopted to address safety but are not themselves coded to the site-safety value, so treat them as motivation evidence rather than as proof of the outcome.

**Detailed answer**

**The asserted route: move the work off site.** Prefabrication/off-site (PR2) enables Improve site safety (VA13), on the reasoning that moving work offsite improves site safety [1], with peer-reviewed evidence [1]. This is an exact statement of the evidence available: VA13 carries 1 inbound and 0 outbound dependency edges, all listed [2], so prefabrication is the single cited enabling path into site safety in this graph. VA13 is nevertheless a very widely coded value: it is activated in 39 of the 50 coded cases [2], while PR2 is activated in 20 of the 50 [2], which means most safety-coded cases reach safety by routes the graph does not assert as dependencies.

**What prefabrication itself requires.** Two preconditions are cited, both peer-reviewed [1]: PR2 dependsOn RI14, since prefabrication relies on precise up-front planning and logistics [2], and PR2 dependsOn RI18, since a functional regulatory system for offsite compliance requires third-party certification and traceability [2]. Feeding it: DfMA (PR9) orients the project toward offsite manufacture [2], early involvement of the delivering production party (CO11) is required to integrate manufacturing and assembly knowledge into design [2], and supply chain integration (VA14) supports the offsite production line [2]. Off-site work also carries adjacent returns: schedule compression (VA2) [2], quality from the controlled factory environment (VA3) [2] and reduced errors and rework (VA10) [2].

**Where the robot stays on site: human-robot interaction.** Human-robot interaction (CO6) is activated in 32 of the 50 coded cases [2] and co-occurs with Improve site safety (VA13) at weight 28 [3], but that is statistical correlation, not an asserted causal path. What CO6 does carry, exactly, is 0 inbound and 3 outbound dependency edges [2], and all three are safety-relevant:

- CO6 dependsOn RI18: human-robot collaborative work depends on compliance with robot safety standards [2], on standards evidence [2].
- CO6 dependsOn RI6: the success of human-robot collaboration is contingent on a skilled workforce, so it depends on addressing workforce training [2], peer-reviewed [3].
- CO6 mitigates RI20: power-and-force-limiting collaborative operation within biomechanical limits mitigates contact-injury risk [2], on standards evidence [4].

So for on-site collaborative work the practical instruction is standards compliance plus operator training plus force-limited operation, rather than an expectation that the robot delivers safety on its own.

**Deployed record.** Three deployed processes in the context name safety as the adoption driver: census_RXM23-1, adopted to address safety, performing drilling on the structural core and sitework, at technology readiness level 7 [4]; census_RXM4-5, adopted to address safety and labor, performing digging and material handling on sitework, substructure and foundation, at technology readiness level 8 [5]; and census_RXM1-3, adopted to address safety and market, performing digging and material handling on sitework, at technology readiness level 8 [6]. These are the hazardous-task substitutions the safety argument rests on in practice: drilling and earthmoving taken off the hands of workers. The context names no firm behind any of the three, and it does not link any of them to the Improve site safety enabler, so they evidence the motivation and the maturity, not the coded outcome. No deployed prefabrication case is present in the material in front of me, so the PR2 to VA13 path here rests on the literature rather than on a named deployment.

**Two cautions on reading the evidence.** First, the long co-occurrence lists around VA13, including its ties to the risk enablers RI1 through RI20 and to values such as human wellbeing, are correlations across cases and carry no direction. 1939 co-occurrence edges touch the enablers reached here and only the 15 strongest are shown [2], so nothing about absence can be read from those lists. Second, the search widened "robotics" across the robotic arm, robotic assembly, unmanned mobile vehicle and gantry senses, and that widening does not add a safety path: the robot arm (RE2) edge runs only to robotic assembly (PR4) [2], and the phase placement of the value is narrow, applying in Structural Construction with a value-realizing role [7].
